scenarios.title: Round-trip standard composite HLA data-element encodings

requirement_mappings.note: The exact encoded vector begins with the one-octet discriminant, its required alignment padding, and the selected HLAinteger32BE alternative bytes. This witnesses this tested alternative combination only.

The registered alternatives have four- and eight-octet boundaries; the test selects the four-octet alternative and verifies seven zero padding octets align it to the maximum boundary. This witnesses this tested padding case only.
The exact vector ends on the selected alternative's final byte and getEncodedLength reports 12, showing no trailing padding for this tested boundary combination.
For the unmapped one-octet discriminant 0x7f, the exact output contains only that byte even though the registered alternatives have an eight-octet maximum boundary; encoded length is one.

With a one-octet HLAbyte discriminant, three zero octets place the four-byte encoded_length at offset four; the exact vector checks its value of four and the following HLAfloat32LE alternative. This witnesses this tested length-field alignment case only.

A Java TCK DataElement reporting a 16-octet boundary is supplied to HLAextendableVariantRecord.setVariant, and the test requires EncoderException. This mirrors rejection of one over-limit alternative boundary only.

The exact bytes encode HLAinteger32BE value 4 and a four-byte selected alternative, showing encoded_length excludes the four alignment octets after the length field. This selected-alternative case does not test the required zero value when no alternative applies.
The exact bytes show four zero octets after the four-octet encoded_length and before the alternative, aligning its offset from 12 to the predefined eight-octet boundary for this selected type pair.

The exact byte vector ends immediately after the four-byte alternative at total size 20, proving this selected encoding adds no trailing padding; getEncodedLength equals the full vector including pre-alternative alignment padding.

The exact bytes begin with the first fixed-record element at output offset zero and encode the two array elements in order, including the required alignment before the second record; this witnesses one fixed cardinality.

The final five-octet record ends at total offset 13 without trailing padding, while the three inter-element alignment octets are included in getEncodedLength; this witnesses one selected array/prototype combination.
The exact bytes start with HLAinteger32BE count 2 at offset zero and then contain the two selected HLAinteger16BE element encodings in order; this checks one nonempty cardinality only.
Exact bytes show the four-octet count followed by four zero padding octets, placing the selected HLAfloat64BE element at offset eight; this witnesses one element-boundary case.

The first five-octet HLAfixedRecord ends at offset nine; three zero octets align the second record to offset twelve, and getEncodedLength includes those inter-element bytes. The final record ends at offset seventeen without trailing padding; other array and record layouts are not covered.

scenarios.mapping_note: The Java encoder round-trip checks a fixed array of two five-octet fixed records, variable-array count and element ordering, variable-array padding before an eight-octet element and between fixed records, focused HLAvariantRecord mapped and unmapped layouts, two HLAextendableVariantRecord vectors for pre-length and post-length padding, and rejection of one custom alternative with a 16-octet boundary. These direct mappings cover only the exact tested Clause 4 cases, not every composite layout or conformance.

scenarios.title: Complete federation execution create, join, query, resign, destroy, and disconnect lifecycle
Preserve case-distinct names and isolate data across executions

requirement_mappings.note: Direct §1.5 p.18 l.58 witness: one connected creator creates and lists two federation executions whose names differ by one ASCII case change; an exact duplicate create is rejected, and one report preserves both exact names. This is one bounded case-variant witness.

Direct §1.5 p.18 l.58 witness: within one execution, a second federate whose name differs by one ASCII case change joins, an exact duplicate is rejected, and one member report preserves both exact names. This is one bounded case-variant witness.

Direct bounded section 4.1 witness: one application process keeps four distinct public RTIambassador sessions joined simultaneously, with two federates in each of two independently named executions; all four joined-federate handles are valid. The scenario then exercises object, interaction, and time services in both executions. This proves the bounded same-process multi-federation participation path, not multiple joins on one ambassador or multi-process behavior.

Direct section 4.5 witness: the public Create Federation Execution service creates two differently named executions; List Federation Executions reports both exact names in one report. This covers the exercised create-and-list behavior, not every create precondition.

Direct bounded section 4.5 independence witness: two executions accept the same two exact federate names, including one ASCII case variant, through separate public RTIambassador sessions. Member reports return exactly those names in each execution; same-execution positive controls and bounded receive-order/TSO isolation checks show the tested behavior remains local to each execution. This is same-process coverage of these membership and delivery paths, not exhaustive service independence.

Direct bounded section 12.8 witness: one connected creator RTIambassador calls Create Federation Execution twice, leaving the first execution live while creating the second, then calls List Federation Executions and receives both in one report. The calls are sequential; this does not claim concurrent invocation of Create Federation Execution.

Direct bounded public-API witness for no intercommunication between federation executions: same-execution controls deliver one receive-order object discovery, attribute reflection, receive-order interaction, and timestamped interaction; the second execution records no corresponding object or receive-order callbacks during a 500 ms window and advances to time 4 with only its grant during the timestamped path. This covers these exercised service paths and does not establish isolation of every service family, transport, independent provider, or process.

scenarios.mapping_note: Direct mappings are bounded to the exercised behavior: clause 1.5 covers one ASCII case variant for federation-execution and federate names, exact-duplicate rejection, and reports preserving both exact spellings; clause 4 covers one application joining multiple federates in two executions, resigning and reusing an ambassador, and tearing down both executions; clause 4.1 covers four distinct public RTIambassador sessions joined simultaneously, two per execution; clause 4.5 covers creating and listing two differently named executions, accepting the same two exact federate names in both with separate member reports, plus same-execution object-discovery and attribute-reflection controls, receive-order and timestamped interaction controls, and bounded peer-isolation checks; clause 12.8 covers one connected creator sequentially creating the second execution while the first remains live and receiving both names in one listing report. The timestamped isolation check is bounded to a peer advance through time 4 that produces only its grant. This is local API evidence, not independent-provider or conformance evidence.

scenarios.title: Preserve transportation handle identity across an additional-FOM join

requirement_mappings.note: The scenario resolves and name-round-trips HLAreliable, HLAbestEffort, the selected model FOM's custom transport, and the extension FOM's custom transport; it verifies shared handles and stable base names after additional-module Join. This is direct but partial evidence for selected name entries only. The official Java API exposes no query for a transportation type's reliability value, so reliability cells and complete arbitrary-FDD table coverage remain unverified.

The scenario proves that the newly joined extension FOM transportation receives one shared handle distinct from HLAreliable, HLAbestEffort, and the base FOM custom type, and that each selected name round-trips. This is direct fixture-bounded evidence for two custom FOM types, not exhaustive proof for every possible transportation declaration.

The scenario retrieves the newly composed transportation from both joined federates using the official Java RTIambassador.getTransportationTypeHandle(name) service and verifies getTransportationTypeName(handle) returns the declared name. This directly exercises the corresponding 2025 Java API service for the selected extension-FOM entry.

The scenario retrieves HLAreliable and HLAbestEffort before and after the additional-FOM join, on both joined federates, and verifies their handles and names remain stable. This is selected runtime preservation evidence, not literal header-file immutability or proof for every possible existing value.

The supplied base and extension FOMs declare the representative custom names TckBestEffort and TckAdditionalTransport. Successful Create/additional-module Join plus public handle/name round-trips provide selected valid-name evidence. The case does not test rejection boundaries or exhaustively test every HLA naming rule in §3.3.

scenarios.mapping_note: The §8.15.3 assertion checks the pending-lookahead formula across two grants: from six epsilon to three after advancing three, then to the requested one epsilon after advancing three more. Zero acceptance is now directly mapped to page 208 l72: the Java test passes a standard zero LogicalTimeInterval to Modify Lookahead, verifies the requested decrease remains pending before a grant, and verifies that Query Lookahead reports zero after the grant. scenarios.title: Deliver a timestamped interaction at the equal-time TARA boundary after its grant

requirement_mappings.note: TARA(5) is granted while the regulator remains at 4 and before it sends an equal-time message at 5; that message is delivered only during a later TARA. This witnesses the clause's no-guarantee rule for all equal-time messages at the first grant in this controlled sequence.

The sender submits a timestamp-5 interaction only after the receiver's first TARA(5) grant, and the receiver gets it after that grant on a later TARA. This directly witnesses a future equal-grant-time message arrival.

Immediately before TARA(5), the receiver queries GALT=5; the request is granted while the time-regulating publisher remains at 4. This directly witnesses a time-constrained request at GALT completing without waiting for the other joined federate to advance.

scenarios.mapping_note: The receiver queries GALT=5 and issues TARA(5) while the publisher remains at 4; the grant arrives before any timestamp-5 interaction exists. Only after that grant does the publisher advance to 5 and send a TSO(5), which the receiver gets after the first grant during a later TARA. This directly covers §8.9 p. 195 l. 119 (the first grant does not guarantee every equal-time message), p. 196 l. 9 (equal-grant-time messages may arrive later), and p. 196 l. 12 (TARA at or below GALT can grant without waiting for another federate). It covers this controlled arrival sequence, distinct from a TSO already queued before the first request and does not generalize to other advance services. Java rebuilt against the pinned IEEE 1516.1-2025 API JAR and passed both callback models with HLAinteger64Time and HLAfloat64Time on the current-source JNI provider (4/4). Installed-package C++ primary and contract runs passed both callback models and both time factories (8/8); the focused CTest query had no registrations. Java traceability export passed all four results, both C++ result bundles validated, Java catalog validation reported 876 scenarios with no findings, and the parity audit found no unpaired Java scenarios. Results: out/java-tck/timestamped-interaction-tara-equal-boundary-port-20261104/. The contract twin reuses the same C++ scenario and is not independent evidence. No Requirements Lab revision or Catch2 plan row changed.

scenarios.title: Verify object-discovery callback response sequence correlation
scenarios.mapping_note: The Java test exercises the public callback-control and object-discovery path through the adapter-supplied TCP endpoint. The independent loopback observer checks HLA_CALL_REQUEST (type 20) and HLA_CALLBACK_RESPONSE (type 23) from federate to RTI, HLA_CALL_RESPONSE (type 21) and HLA_CALLBACK_REQUEST (type 22) from RTI to federate, and pairs each callback response to the request sequence on the same connection and session. The observer also checks the four-byte big-endian In response to value and successful CallbackSucceeded protobuf. Scope is limited to this object-discovery route and does not imply coverage of every callback family or failure encoding.
scenarios.callback_model_scope_note: Both Java callback models run the same two-ambassador object-discovery path; the adapter checks the wire direction and sequence correlation for the callback response in each run.

scenarios.title: Reject an unpublished-target HLAmodifyAttributeState request, report it to the manager, then verify the published transfer

requirement_mappings.note: After the target publishes the application attribute, the same HLAmodifyAttributeState request transfers ownership without ownership callbacks. This direct mapping covers only that successful transfer.

The test checks the service, managing federate, false HLAparameterError, exact standard parameter set, reliable transport, empty tag, no producing federate, and no regions.

OrderType is checked separately as a distinct API enum value, not treated as a Handle. Finite observations establish uniqueness for these names but do not prove unpredictability.

The scenario encodes 11 named handle-valued FDD designators, destroys the first execution, creates a second execution on the same RTI with the same FDD file, and asserts the same names return the same encodings. This is a bounded observation for the listed names, not every possible FDD.

The test creates two federation executions using the same RTI version and the same FDD path and compares the encoded values for the same 11 FDD-derived names. It directly exercises the stated cross-execution condition; it does not claim independent-provider interoperability or universal coverage of all names.

The first execution asserts pairwise distinct encoded values for representative object-class, attribute, interaction-class, parameter, dimension, and transportation-type handles, directly checking execution-wide uniqueness for those names.

scenarios.mapping_note: The Java counterpart checks the same six handle-valued FOM categories, pairwise encoded-handle uniqueness, identical same-execution values across two federates, fixed OrderType enum identity, and repeatability of the same 11 FDD-derived encodings across successive executions on the same connected RTI instance. Focused Java current-source JNI runs and C++ installed-package CTests passed under HLA_EVOKED and HLA_IMMEDIATE. These are local-provider/API-surface results, not independent-provider interoperability or conformance.

scenarios.title: preserve case-sensitive FOM names across public handle lookups

requirement_mappings.note: The fom-root-classes-omitted-tck.xml fixture declares TckObject and TckInteraction without explicitly declaring HLAobjectRoot or HLAinteractionRoot. After joining with the standard MIM, both standard root names and the fully qualified subclass names resolve through the public API.

In the portable P0 FOM, the complete object and interaction class names resolve, while their unqualified leaf names throw NameNotFound; the standard HLA object and interaction root classes also resolve by their root names. This is bounded to one non-root class in each hierarchy.

Using the portable P0 FOM, exact-case object-class, attribute, interaction-class, and parameter lookups round-trip to their names; changing the first character's case makes each lookup throw NameNotFound. This is a direct but bounded witness for these four name categories.

For §12.2 p353-l66-21, the public C++ scenario exercises the Clause 10 name/handle lookup pattern for object classes, attributes, interaction classes, and parameters: a FOM name resolves to a handle and that handle resolves back to the exact name. This is bounded service evidence; dimension, order, transportation, update-rate, object-instance, and any other name families require separate evidence.

Selected valid-name witness only: the P0 FOM's HLAinteractionRoot.TckInteraction is accepted and round-trips through public handle/name lookup with exact-case semantics. Qualified identity is exercised separately by cpp-tck.fom-interaction-qualified-class-name-identity; malformed-name rejection and the full §3.3 rule set are not claimed.

scenarios.mapping_note: The focused Java scenario covers the P0 fixture's complete object and interaction class names, root names, unqualified leaf rejection, exact-case round trips, and first-letter case-mismatch rejection for object class, attribute, interaction class, and parameter. It also checks standard root and fully qualified subclass lookups against the root-class-omitted FOM fixture. Other support lookup, handle identity, and encoding assertions in java-tck.support-services are outside this parity link. The direct C++ mappings remain the source rows; this Java parity link adds no interoperability or conformance claim.

scenarios.title: decode a valid object-instance handle without checking local federation membership
scenarios.mapping_note: The Java test encodes an object-instance handle in one federation, decodes it through a joined RTI in another federation, and confirms that the typed value survives while the target federation name lookup reports ObjectInstanceNotKnown. This directly maps p. 382 l. 27-8 to §12.12.4.2 for object-instance handle decoding only; no other handle factory is implied.

scenarios.title: round-trip public handle encodings as standard HLAbyte variable arrays
scenarios.mapping_note: The Java test encodes the ten standard handle kinds as HLAvariableArray<HLAbyte> values and round-trips each through its corresponding Java HandleFactory. This maps p. 382 l. 24-7 to §12.12.4.2; it does not claim C++-specific cross-federate reconstitution or other handle requirements.

scenarios.title: preserve and reconstitute an object-instance handle through interaction and attribute value maps

requirement_mappings.note: The Java sender places ObjectInstanceHandle.encode() bytes in an interaction parameter; the receiver verifies byte preservation before using the matching Java ObjectInstanceHandleFactory. This exercises one standard handle-as-parameter path.
The receiver decodes the parameter bytes with ObjectInstanceHandleFactory and confirms that the reconstituted handle and resolved object name match the registered instance.
The receiver requires the other eight standard Java handle factories to reject these object-instance bytes with CouldNotDecode; this is bounded to the tested public factories and encoding.

For receive-order Send Interaction and Update Attribute Values, the receiver holds callbacks while the service returns. The sender then mutates the byte[] value still held in each caller-owned map; the receiver must get the original bytes. This is bounded to these two input-map routes.

The same ObjectInstanceHandle encoding is placed in one ParameterHandleValueMap and one AttributeHandleValueMap. The receiver checks exact bytes and reconstitutes the handle through ObjectInstanceHandleFactory. Other handle types and value-map paths are not claimed.

scenarios.mapping_note: The Java case sends a registered ObjectInstanceHandle encoding in both an interaction parameter and an attribute value, verifies byte-preserving receive, decodes each value with ObjectInstanceHandleFactory, and confirms the same object name. Eight other standard Java handle factories must reject the encoding with CouldNotDecode. For both receive-order services the receiver holds callbacks until the call returns; the sender then mutates the caller-owned byte[] in the input map, and the receiver must still get the original bytes. Direct mappings cover p. 353 l. 120, 123, and 132-43 -> §12.2, p. 377 l. 210-68 -> §12.11.7, and p. 396 l. 186-61 -> §12.13.3.3. Scope is one object-instance handle and the tested ParameterHandleValueMap/AttributeHandleValueMap services; no private message encoding, other handle classes, or other value-map routes are claimed.
scenarios.evidence_note: Compiled against the pinned IEEE 1516.1-2025 Java API JAR. scenarios.title: select standard logical-time factories by default and implementation name
scenarios.mapping_note: The Java test checks the default float64 factory, both standardized factory names, the unknown-name result, and initial time zero. It maps p. 378 l. 261-86 and l. 306-101 to §12.12.1.1. The C++-specific installed-header placement assertion at l. 339-112 is not ported.

scenarios.title: reject negative intervals for both standard logical-time representations
scenarios.mapping_note: The Java test checks zero and positive interval controls and requires negative integer64 and float64 intervals to be rejected. This directly maps p. 176 l. 22-7 to §8.1.1. It does not assert a checked exception class or claim the separate FOM-schema mapping.

scenarios.title: discover a derived object and reflect its inherited attribute through a base-class subscription
scenarios.mapping_note: The Java scenario uses the same typed hierarchy and inherited Identity attribute through the official IEEE 1516.1-2025 Java API. scenarios.exclusion: Opt-in Java TCK scenario: RtiTckMain registers defaultEnabled=false, so it is reported unsupported by the default suite unless selected through a capability profile or enabled with -Dhla.rti.tck.runUnverified=true.

exclusions.scope: C++ VariableLengthData ownership and pointer-storage contract
exclusions.reason: IEEE 1516.1-2025 Java exposes byte arrays and DataElement values rather than a VariableLengthData class or pointer-adoption API. Java Credentials also exposes its backing array, so C++ copy/assignment ownership semantics are not portable Java assertions.

exclusions.scope: C++ clone/copy, dynamic-type, and vector-offset assertions for logical-time DataElements
exclusions.reason: The Java API exposes HLAlogicalTime and HLAlogicalTimeInterval DataElement wrappers, and java-tck.logical-time-data-elements-contract covers their Java-visible value, encoding, decoding, boundary, cursor, and malformed-input behavior. C++ clone/copy independence, dynamic-type compatibility overloads, and vector encodeInto/decodeFrom(offset) have no Java API counterpart and remain excluded.

exclusions.scope: Provider implementation classes and implementation-only state-machine tests
exclusions.reason: The portable Java TCK may change only API/provider JARs, factory name, FOM/MIM inputs, and capability profile. Provider implementation evidence remains in the provider's own compliance lane.

exclusions.scope: Provider-internal transport, persistence, allocator, and authorization implementation details
exclusions.reason: Only behavior observable through hla.rti1516_2025 is portable; implementation-specific evidence remains in the provider's own compliance lane.

exclusions.scope: Per-join report-file allocation, filesystem identity/contents, and report append policy across restore
exclusions.reason: The portable negotiated ownership and save/restore behavior is covered by java-tck.pending-negotiated-ownership-save-restore, and the standard public HLAreportServiceFile value is covered separately by java-tck.federate-mom-report-service-file. Exact paths, distinct files per join, file-set stability, filesystem contents, and append-gating are provider implementation details and are not portable HLA assertions.

exclusions.reason: The candidate has no direct normative clause mapping. Filesystem failure injection, RTIinternalError classification, fallback policy, and retry after repair are provider-specific behaviors, not portable IEEE 1516.1-2025 TCK assertions.

exclusions.reason: The candidate has no direct normative clause mapping. Filesystem failure injection, exception classification, failed-join rollback/discovery policy, and retry after repair are provider-specific behaviors, not portable IEEE 1516.1-2025 TCK assertions.
